stem: Three product teams in one AWS account call the same Amazon Bedrock model. Finance wants each team's Bedrock spend shown separately in AWS Cost Explorer and an email when a team's forecast spend for the month reaches 80 percent of its budget. What should the ML engineer do?

choices.text: Have each team call the model through its own application inference profile tagged `team`, activate the tag for cost allocation, and set tag-filtered budgets
Add a `team` tag to the shared foundation model's ARN and activate it for cost allocation, because tags on the model ID split its token charges between the calling teams
Enable model invocation logging and build a CloudWatch dashboard of each team's prompts, because Cost Explorer reads the logged token counts to split the charges by team
Create a separate Provisioned Throughput for each team and tag it, because on-demand Bedrock usage in an account cannot be divided between teams in any way

stem: A logistics company extracts 12 fields from delivery notes with a large Amazon Bedrock model. Accuracy is 97 percent on a labeled test set of 800 notes, and the business requires at least 95 percent. Monthly cost is too high, and a smaller model from the same family costs a fraction as much per token. What should the ML engineer do?

choices.text: Keep the large model and lower the temperature to zero, because deterministic sampling reduces the price that is charged for each output token of the response
Move the large model to Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment, because committed capacity always costs less than on-demand calls for any traffic level
Evaluate the smaller model on the same 800 labeled notes with a Bedrock evaluation job and switch if it reaches 95 percent, keeping that test set for later checks
Fine-tune the large model on the 800 labeled notes, because a customized model is billed at a lower per-token rate than the base model that it was trained from

stem: A team's Amazon Bedrock knowledge base indexes 300,000 product documents from Amazon S3; about 500 change each day. Embedding costs are far higher than expected. The nightly job deletes the data source, recreates it, and starts an ingestion job. How should the ML engineer reduce the embedding cost?

choices.text: Replace the nightly job with a weekly full rebuild, because a knowledge base charges embedding cost only once per week for each document regardless of how often it changes
Keep the data source and only start an ingestion job on it each night, because a sync processes just the documents that were added, changed or deleted since the last one
Keep the nightly job but switch to an embedding model with a larger vector dimension, because larger vectors need fewer embedding calls for each document that is ingested
Move the documents to a second S3 bucket every night before the job, because a knowledge base ingests only the objects that are new in a bucket it has not seen yet

stem: An HR assistant on Amazon Bedrock must refuse questions about planned layoffs and must never show employees' US Social Security numbers that appear in retrieved HR records. Which TWO Amazon Bedrock Guardrails settings should the ML engineer configure? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A prompt attack filter at HIGH strength, so that questions about layoffs and requests for ID numbers are classified as jailbreaks
A content filter for the misconduct category at HIGH strength, so that any message mentioning layoffs or ID numbers is filtered
A denied topic for workforce reductions, with a clear definition and sample phrases, so related questions and answers are blocked
A contextual grounding check with a high grounding threshold, so answers about layoffs that the documents do not support are blocked
A sensitive information filter for the US Social Security number type, set to mask or block it in model responses for every user

stem: A developer created a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key while trying out models and now wants to put the same key into the environment variables of a production Lambda function that calls the Converse API. What should the ML engineer recommend?

choices.text: Create an IAM user with an access key for the function, because an access key that is rotated every 90 days is safer than any role for production Bedrock calls
Keep the long-term API key but store it in AWS Secrets Manager, because a key read from a secret at run time is the AWS recommended credential for production workloads
Generate a short-term API key once during deployment and place it in the environment variables, because short-term keys never expire while the function is unchanged
Grant Bedrock permissions to the function's execution role and call with the SDK, so it uses temporary credentials, and keep API keys for exploration only

stem: An ML application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets that have no NAT gateway or internet gateway. It must call Amazon Bedrock models, and the security team requires that Bedrock runtime calls made with the application's role be denied unless they arrive through the company's network path. What should the ML engineer do?

choices.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for `bedrock-runtime` with private DNS, and add a policy statement that denies Bedrock calls whose `aws:SourceVpce` is not that endpoint
Request a VPC peering connection to the Amazon Bedrock service VPC, and allow only the peered CIDR range in the security groups of the application's EC2 instances
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon Bedrock and add it to the route tables, and attach an S3 bucket policy that allows only requests from that gateway endpoint
Create an interface VPC endpoint for the `bedrock` control plane service only, because model invocation requests are sent through the same endpoint as management calls

stem: A pharmaceutical company fine-tunes a model with an Amazon Bedrock model customization job on confidential trial documents. Security requires that the resulting custom model be encrypted with a key the company controls and can disable, which would make the model unusable. What should the ML engineer do?

choices.text: Store the custom model weights in AWS CloudHSM after training, because Bedrock can serve a custom model only from keys that are held in a dedicated HSM cluster
Specify a customer managed KMS key for the custom model in the customization job and allow the job's service role and model users to use that key in its key policy
Encrypt the training data bucket with SSE-S3 managed keys, because the custom model inherits the encryption setting of the bucket that held its training data
Rely on the default AWS owned key that Bedrock uses for custom models, and remove the training data from S3 after the job to protect the confidential documents

stem: An ML engineer is hardening an agent that reads incoming customer emails and can call two tools: one that queries the order database and one that sends emails. A red team showed that an email with hidden instructions can make the agent send order data to an outside address. Which TWO measures BEST reduce the impact of such prompt injection? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions found inside emails, and rely on it as the main control against injected instructions
Encrypt the incoming emails with a customer managed KMS key before the agent reads them, so injected instructions cannot be interpreted by the model
Give the database tool read-only access to only the order fields the agent needs, and scope the email tool to send only to the customer on the current case
Enable model invocation logging, because recording each prompt and response lets the agent block injected instructions before the email tool is called
Require a human approval step before the email tool sends any message that contains order data or goes to an address outside the current case

stem: An ML team builds the container image for a SageMaker AI inference endpoint in AWS CodeBuild and pushes it to Amazon ECR. Security wants known vulnerabilities in the operating system and Python packages of each image found before deployment, failing the build when a critical finding appears. What should the ML engineer use?

choices.text: Amazon Macie on the ECR repository, because it inspects image layers for vulnerable packages and fails the CodeBuild project when a critical finding appears
AWS Config rules on the ECR repository, because each image push is evaluated for vulnerable packages and the build is stopped when the image is non-compliant
Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring on the endpoint, because it reports vulnerable Python packages in the image and stops the build before the image is pushed
Amazon Inspector scanning in the CodeBuild stage, failing the build on critical findings, plus Inspector enhanced scanning of the ECR repository after the push

stem: A support assistant sends Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs to a CloudWatch Logs log group so engineers can debug. Prompts often contain customers' email addresses and credit card numbers. Security wants engineers to keep reading the logs but see those values hidden, with only a small incident team able to view them. What should the ML engineer do?

choices.text: Attach a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy that masks email and card numbers, and grant `logs:Unmask` only to the incident team's role
Encrypt the log group with a customer managed KMS key, because encrypted log events are shown to engineers with the email addresses and card numbers hidden
Run Amazon Macie on the log group every day, because Macie finds the sensitive values in log events and replaces them with masked text in place
Turn off text delivery in the invocation logging settings, so that prompts and responses are no longer written to the log group that the engineers use

stem: A retailer must generate marketing summaries for about two million product records every night with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Results are needed by the next morning, nobody waits on an individual response, and the team wants the lowest cost per token. Which deployment option fits best?

choices.text: Buy Bedrock Provisioned Throughput with a one-month commitment and send the records through InvokeModel calls from a fleet of Lambda functions.
Submit a Bedrock batch inference job that reads the records as JSONL files from Amazon S3 and writes the model outputs to an S3 output prefix.
Call the model on demand through a cross-Region inference profile so that the nightly burst of requests is spread over Regions without throttling.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with auto scaling and loop through all the records from one EC2 instance during the night.

stem: A US healthcare analytics company calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1 with on-demand throughput. During afternoon peaks some requests are throttled. Compliance requires that inference stays inside the United States, and the team does not want to commit to reserved capacity. What should the ML engineer change?

choices.text: Set the modelId to the US geographic cross-Region inference profile, so Bedrock can route requests to other US Regions in the profile during peaks.
Set the modelId to the global cross-Region inference profile, so Bedrock can route requests to any commercial Region that has spare capacity.
Deploy a second copy of the application in us-west-2 and add client-side logic that switches Regions after every throttling error it receives.
Buy Provisioned Throughput with a six-month commitment in us-east-1 sized for the afternoon peak and send all traffic to the provisioned model.

stem: An ML team hosts four fine-tuned 8B-parameter open-weight LLMs, each on its own SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a 4-GPU instance. Each model needs only one GPU and gets little traffic. Two models use a different serving container than the others. The team wants one endpoint where each model keeps its own resources and scales on its own. What should they use?

choices.text: Move the models to SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoints, which share one pool of GPU capacity and charge only for the time each model is processing a request.
Deploy the models on one multi-model endpoint, which loads each model from Amazon S3 on demand and scales the copies of each model with its own target-tracking policy.
Deploy the models as a multi-container endpoint with direct invocation, where each container receives its own GPU and an independent auto scaling policy per container.
Deploy each model as an inference component on one endpoint, giving each component its own accelerator and memory allocation and its own copy-count scaling policy.

stem: A legal-tech company serves an open-weight LLM on a SageMaker AI asynchronous inference endpoint. Requests carry document bundles of up to 200 MB and take 5 to 15 minutes each. To save cost, the auto scaling minimum is 0 and a target-tracking policy uses the backlog size per instance. After a quiet night at zero instances, new requests stay queued and no instance starts. What should the ML engineer change?

choices.text: Increase the invocation timeout of the asynchronous endpoint to its maximum, so that the queued requests are kept long enough for an instance to start.
Set the minimum instance count back to 1, so that one GPU instance stays running through the night and picks up the first requests in the morning.
Add a step scaling policy driven by a CloudWatch alarm on the endpoint's backlog-without-capacity metric, so that queued requests start the first instance.
Lower the target value of the target-tracking policy to one queued request per instance, so that a single waiting request triggers a scale-out.

stem: An ML engineer must host a 70B-parameter open-weight LLM on SageMaker AI. In 16-bit precision the weights need about 140 GB, more than the memory of any single GPU on the chosen ml.p4d.24xlarge instance (eight GPUs with 40 GB each). What is the most direct way to serve the model?

choices.text: Use the generic PyTorch inference container with an initial instance count of 4, so the endpoint spreads the model's weights across four instances.
Use a SageMaker AI large model inference (LMI) container and set the tensor parallel degree to 8, so the model's layers are split across all eight GPUs.
Use a SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint with its largest memory setting, so the weights are paged in from Amazon S3 as each layer is needed.
Use the SageMaker distributed data parallel library at inference time, so each request batch is split across the eight GPUs of the instance.

stem: A support chatbot has two back ends: a Claude model on Amazon Bedrock and a fine-tuned open model on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that uses an LMI container with streaming enabled. Users complain that each reply appears only after the whole answer is generated. Which TWO API calls should the application use so tokens appear as they are produced? (Select TWO)

choices.text: InvokeEndpointAsync on the SageMaker AI Runtime API, which returns the generated tokens through an Amazon SNS topic while the model is running.
StartAsyncInvoke on the Bedrock Runtime API, which keeps the HTTP connection open and pushes partial output to the client until generation ends.
InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream on the SageMaker AI Runtime API, which returns the container's output in parts as the model generates it.
CreateModelInvocationJob on the Bedrock API, which streams the output of each record to the client as soon as the job has processed that record.
ConverseStream on the Bedrock Runtime API, which returns the model output as a stream of events while the text is still being generated.

stem: An insurance company runs a claims-triage assistant on Amazon Bedrock around the clock. Traffic is steady and well forecast for the next year, and the business requires a guaranteed level of throughput for this model instead of shared on-demand capacity. Which option meets the requirement?

choices.text: Run Bedrock batch inference jobs every few minutes, which reserve dedicated capacity for the account while the records of each job are being processed.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with a commitment term, sized in model units for the forecast load, and invoke it through the provisioned model ARN.
Use on-demand invocation through a cross-Region inference profile, which reserves a fixed share of capacity in each Region of the profile for the account.
Raise the on-demand tokens-per-minute quota through Service Quotas, which turns the shared on-demand capacity into capacity dedicated to the account.

stem: A team deploys a Bedrock knowledge base with AWS CloudFormation: an AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase resource with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store, and an AWS::Bedrock::DataSource resource for an S3 bucket that already holds the documents. The stack creates successfully, but Retrieve calls return no results. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The data source has never been synchronized; add a pipeline step or custom resource that calls StartIngestionJob after the stack deploys.
The embedding model needs Provisioned Throughput before it can embed documents; buy model units and reference them in the knowledge base.
CloudFormation cannot attach S3 data sources to knowledge bases; recreate the data source by hand in the console after every stack deployment.
The vector index stays empty until OpenSearch Serverless copies it to a standby collection; wait for that replication and then query again.

stem: A team's production application calls Amazon Bedrock with a guardrail but references the guardrail's working draft. An engineer tuned a content filter in the console for a test, and the change affected production at once. The team wants guardrail changes reviewed in Git and production to change only when a release is deployed. What should they do?

choices.text: Attach the guardrail to an application inference profile and tag the profile with a version, so the profile freezes the guardrail settings at the tagged time.
Copy the guardrail to a second AWS Region for production and call it through a cross-Region inference profile, so edits in the first Region never reach it.
Define the guardrail in CloudFormation and enable stack termination protection, so console edits to the draft are blocked while the application keeps using it.
Define the guardrail with AWS::Bedrock::Guardrail and publish AWS::Bedrock::GuardrailVersion resources in CloudFormation, and have production reference a specific version.

stem: A startup is building its first production AI agent with the open-source LangGraph framework and a model on Amazon Bedrock. It wants managed, serverless hosting in which each user session runs isolated from other sessions, sessions can run long multi-step tasks, and the team keeps its framework code. Which service should host the agent?

choices.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents (Classic), which imports LangGraph graphs as action groups and runs them on managed capacity separately for each session.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, which hosts agent code built with any framework and runs each user session in its own isolated environment.
Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Inference, which hosts the agent's container and keeps each session's state on the endpoint between invocations.
Amazon Bedrock Flows, which converts LangGraph code into a flow definition and runs each user session through a separate alias of that flow.

stem: An agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime must call a company's existing REST APIs and AWS Lambda functions as tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) without writing an MCP server for each one. It must also remember each customer's preferences across separate conversations. Which TWO AgentCore capabilities meet these needs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AgentCore Code Interpreter, which wraps existing REST APIs in generated code so that the agent can call them as MCP tools.
AgentCore Identity, which stores each customer's preferences together with the user identity so that the agent can read them later.
AgentCore Browser, which caches each customer's earlier conversations in a managed browser profile that the agent reopens later.
AgentCore Gateway, which turns existing APIs and Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools that the agent can discover and call.
AgentCore Memory, which stores conversation events as short-term memory and extracts long-term memory such as user preferences.

stem: An ML application in private subnets calls InvokeModel on Amazon Bedrock. Security requires this traffic to use AWS PrivateLink instead of the NAT gateway. The team created an interface VPC endpoint for the bedrock-runtime service, but VPC Flow Logs show the calls still leave through the NAT gateway. The application uses the default SDK endpoint. What is the most likely fix?

choices.text: Enable private DNS on the interface endpoint, so the default bedrock-runtime hostname resolves to the private IP addresses of the endpoint in the VPC.
Attach an endpoint policy that allows bedrock:InvokeModel, because an interface endpoint without a policy sends its traffic through the NAT gateway.
Create the interface endpoint for the bedrock service instead, because model invocation calls are served by the Bedrock control-plane endpoint.
Add a gateway VPC endpoint for Bedrock to the private route tables, because interface endpoints for Bedrock carry only control-plane API calls.

stem: A team defines a GenAI application with the AWS CDK in TypeScript: a Bedrock guardrail, a knowledge base and several Lambda functions. The security team wants every pull request to fail if the synthesized template contains a guardrail without a sensitive information (PII) filter. Which approach catches this before anything is deployed?

choices.text: Turn on CloudFormation drift detection for the production stack and fail the pull request whenever the deployed guardrail differs from its template.
Add a CloudWatch alarm on the guardrail's intervention metrics and roll back the stack when no PII interventions are recorded for a full day.
Write unit tests with the CDK assertions module that synthesize the stack and check the guardrail's properties, and run them in the pull-request build.
Run cdk diff against the production account in the build and require reviewers to read the output for missing guardrail filters on each change.

stem: An ML team fine-tunes a model on Amazon Bedrock each month. A workflow must start the model customization job, wait for it to finish (which can take many hours), then run an evaluation and notify the team. The team does not want to write custom polling code. Which design fits?

choices.text: An Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule that starts the job, plus a second schedule a fixed 24 hours later that starts the evaluation whatever the job status.
A SageMaker Pipelines training step that points at the Bedrock base model ID, so that SageMaker AI runs the Bedrock customization job and waits for it.
An AWS Step Functions state machine that uses the Bedrock CreateModelCustomizationJob integration with the .sync pattern, followed by evaluation and notification states.
An AWS Lambda function that starts the customization job and loops on GetModelCustomizationJob with a sleep between checks until the job reports completion.

stem: Several teams upload policy documents during the day to an S3 bucket that backs a Bedrock knowledge base. The ML engineer must refresh the knowledge base every night after the upload window closes, then run a retrieval quality check and alert on failure. Which design fits best?

choices.text: An S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function for every uploaded object, and each invocation calls StartIngestionJob and runs the quality check right after the call returns.
An EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts a Step Functions workflow that calls StartIngestionJob, polls GetIngestionJob in a Wait and Choice loop until it completes, then runs the check.
A SageMaker AI Processing job re-embeds all documents each night and writes the vectors into the knowledge base's S3 data source bucket, then runs the quality check.
A nightly schedule redeploys the CloudFormation stack of the knowledge base, because updating the AWS::Bedrock::DataSource resource re-embeds every document in the bucket.

stem: A team stores prompt templates in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Developers keep editing the draft, but production must use a tested prompt until a release changes it, and each release must be traceable to an exact prompt text. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Have the application reference the prompt's draft ARN and use IAM so that developers can edit the draft only during release windows.
Tag the prompt with the release number, which makes Bedrock freeze the template text that was current at the moment the tag was added.
Export the prompt to Amazon S3 at each release with S3 Versioning turned on, which makes Bedrock load the newest exported object.
Create a prompt version at each release, which saves an immutable snapshot of the draft's template text and its inference settings.
Have the application reference the prompt ARN with the version number, for example as the modelId in a Converse API call.

stem: A team builds a document-classification workflow with Amazon Bedrock Flows. Releases must move from test to production without code changes in the calling application, and a bad release must be rolled back within minutes. How should the application call the flow?

choices.text: Invoke the flow through a production alias, and at each release point the alias to a newly created immutable flow version, or back to the previous version.
Create a new flow for every release and store its flow ID in the application's environment variables, then redeploy the application to switch.
Invoke the flow through a cross-Region inference profile, which keeps the previous flow definition available as a fallback for rollback.
Invoke the working draft of the flow, and at each release prepare the draft again after merging the tested changes from the test account into it.

stem: A CodePipeline pipeline promotes a new prompt version and a new guardrail version of a Bedrock-based assistant from staging to production. The team wants the pipeline to block promotion automatically when answer quality or safety regresses. Which TWO stages should be added before the production deployment? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A CodeBuild action that runs cfn-lint on the templates and fails the stage if the guardrail or prompt resources contain syntax errors or unknown property names.
A manual approval action in which a reviewer reads the change summary of the pipeline and approves the release when the commit messages say the changes were tested.
A CloudWatch alarm on the invocation errors of the production application that rolls back the stack if errors rise during the first hour after the deployment.
A CodeBuild action that runs an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job, for example LLM-as-a-judge, on a golden prompt set and fails the stage if scores fall below agreed thresholds.
A CodeBuild action that sends a red-team prompt set through the ApplyGuardrail API with the new guardrail version and fails the stage if any harmful content is not blocked.

stem: A SageMaker Pipelines workflow fine-tunes an open-weight model from SageMaker JumpStart, evaluates it, and registers passing models in the SageMaker Model Registry with status PendingManualApproval. When a reviewer approves a model package, deployment to the production inference component must start automatically. How should the deployment be triggered?

choices.text: An Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the SageMaker model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus Approved and starts the deployment pipeline.
An S3 event notification on the model artifact bucket, which fires when the reviewer approves the package because approval rewrites the model artifact.
A condition step at the end of the SageMaker pipeline that waits until the reviewer approves the package and then deploys it in the same pipeline execution.
A CloudWatch alarm on an approved-packages count for the Model Registry, which starts the deployment pipeline through an alarm action when the count rises.

stem: A team deploys an AI agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime from a container image. Its CodePipeline currently rebuilds the image separately in the staging stage and in the production stage. A production failure was traced to a dependency version that changed between the two builds. What should the team change?

choices.text: Keep separate builds but pin the base image to the latest tag in both stages, so staging and production always pull the same newest base layers.
Deploy production directly from the source repository with a separate CodeBuild project that runs the same build commands as the staging stage.
Build the image once, push it to Amazon ECR, and deploy that same image digest to staging and then, after the staging tests pass, to production.
Rebuild the image in production with the CodeBuild cache enabled, so that the dependency layers are reused from the staging build automatically.
